title: Memory and Latency Numbers
summary: The memory hierarchy from registers to the other side of the world, the latency numbers you reason with in every design, and why locality makes caches work.

questions.prompt: Put these in order from fastest to slowest and give a rough latency for each: SSD random read, L1 cache hit, round trip within a datacenter, RAM access, HDD seek, round trip from California to Europe.
questions.hint: Think ns → µs → ms. Each step is roughly 100× to 1000×.
keyPoints: L1 cache hit ≈ 1 ns
RAM access ≈ 100 ns
SSD random read ≈ tens to ~100 µs
Datacenter round trip ≈ 0.5 ms (500 µs)
HDD seek ≈ 5–10 ms, then California–Europe round trip ≈ 150 ms
Gets the order right and recognizes the gaps are orders of magnitude

questions.prompt: A service reads user profiles. A Redis lookup costs 0.5 ms; a database read on a miss costs 10 ms (and the Redis check still happens first). What is the average latency at an 80% hit rate? At 98%? What does that tell you about hit rates?
questions.hint: average = cache time + miss rate × database time.
keyPoints: Going from 80% to 98% hit rate makes the average about 3.5× faster
Misses dominate the average, so small hit-rate gains matter a lot
Also notes the database load drops from 20% to 2% of requests (10× fewer DB reads)
questions.answer: 80%: `0.5 + 0.2 × 10 = 2.5 ms`. 98%: `0.5 + 0.02 × 10 = 0.7 ms`. Misses dominate; and DB traffic drops 10× (20% → 2% of requests).

questions.prompt: An order-history page takes 400 ms. Tracing shows: one query to fetch 100 orders, then one query per order to fetch its items, each about 3 ms, done one after another. What is this problem called, and how would you fix it? Estimate the latency after the fix.
questions.hint: Count the round trips. What if you fetched all the items in one go?
keyPoints: This is the N+1 query problem: 1 query for the list plus N queries for details
About 100 × 3 ms ≈ 300 ms is spent on sequential round trips
Fix: one batched query (WHERE order_id IN (...)) or a JOIN, or a data loader that batches
After the fix: roughly 2 queries ≈ 6–10 ms, plus the rest of the page's work
Explains that the cost is per-round-trip latency, not data volume
questions.answer: N+1 queries: `100 × 3 ms ≈ 300 ms` of the 400 ms. Batch with `WHERE order_id IN (...)` or a JOIN → 2 queries ≈ 6 ms, so the page drops to about 100 ms or less.

questions.prompt: You need to scan a 500 GB log file once. Estimate how long it takes if it is on (a) an HDD at 200 MB/s, (b) an NVMe SSD at 4 GB/s, (c) a remote machine over a 10 Gbps link. What is the bottleneck in each case?
questions.hint: Watch bits vs bytes for the network.
keyPoints: HDD: 500,000 MB / 200 MB/s = 2,500 s ≈ 42 minutes
NVMe: 500 GB / 4 GB/s = 125 s ≈ 2 minutes
10 Gbps = 1.25 GB/s, so 500 / 1.25 = 400 s ≈ 7 minutes
Bottleneck is disk throughput for (a), likely CPU parsing or the SSD for (b), network bandwidth for (c)
Mentions sequential reads are what make these rates possible; random access would be far slower

questions.hint: How far apart in memory are two consecutive reads in each version? How big is a cache line?
keyPoints: b is slower: its inner loop jumps N × 8 bytes = 32 KB between reads
a reads memory sequentially, so each 64-byte cache line serves 8 doubles and the prefetcher helps
b gets a cache miss on almost every read, paying RAM latency (~100 ns) instead of cache latency
Same Big-O (N^2), different constant factors because of spatial locality
questions.answer: `b` is slower. `a` walks memory in order (stride 8 bytes), so one 64-byte cache line serves 8 reads and the prefetcher streams ahead. `b`'s inner loop jumps `4096 × 8 = 32 KB` per read, so nearly every read is a cache miss costing RAM latency (~100 ns) instead of ~1 ns.

questions.prompt: Your product is hosted only in `us-east` (Virginia). Users in Singapore (about 15,500 km away) complain the app feels slow: each page needs 4 sequential API calls. Using the speed of light in fiber, estimate the minimum network time per page, and propose what you'd change.
questions.hint: Light in fiber is about 200,000 km/s. A round trip covers the distance twice. Real routes are longer than straight lines.
keyPoints: One-way ≥ 15,500 / 200,000 s ≈ 78 ms, round trip ≥ ~155 ms (real-world ~200–250 ms)
4 sequential calls ≥ ~620 ms of pure network time, before TLS/TCP handshakes
Reduce round trips: batch calls into one, or parallelize independent calls
Move content closer: CDN for static assets and cacheable responses, edge termination of TLS
For dynamic data consider a regional deployment with read replicas in Asia, noting the consistency/complexity trade-off
questions.answer: `15,500 km / 200,000 km/s ≈ 78 ms` one way → `≥ 155 ms` RTT. Four sequential calls `≥ 620 ms`. Batch or parallelize calls, put a CDN/edge in front, and consider an Asia region with read replicas.
